title: Umar's letter on judging
hookLine: judge with understanding, treat both sides equally, the claimant brings proof
tomorrow: a stranger isn't your brother. so what is he to you?

lines: A LETTER FOR THE JUDGE'S SEAT.
cards: Two friends, one argument, and both are texting you their side. Each version is airtight. Each one ends: you agree, right?

Being the judge feels like a trap: agree with one and lose the other, stay quiet and lose both. Umar ibn al-Khattab wrote a letter for exactly this seat, to Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, a judge he had appointed.

teach.h: A RIGHT MUST BE CARRIED OUT.
teach.b: The letter is short and packed. Judging, Umar says, is a firm duty. Understand what's brought to you, because a right that isn't carried out does no good.

Then the line at its heart: treat people as equals in how you look at them, where you seat them and how you judge them, so the powerful don't hope for your favor and the weak don't despair of your fairness.
The one who makes a claim must bring the proof; the one who denies takes an oath.
Don't let a judgment you made yesterday stop you from returning to what's right after you've thought again, because returning to the truth is better than staying in a wrong.
And understanding, understanding, he repeats, when a case isn't plainly settled in the Qur'an or the Sunna. Last: keep anger and irritation out of the courtroom. Now bring it into the group chat.

teach.h: THE SAME FACE TO BOTH SIDES.
teach.b: Equal in how you look means one friend doesn't get the warmer face.
The claimant brings proof means the loudest text doesn't win.
And the line about yesterday means even your first opinion can change.
Umar wrote for courts. It fits a kitchen table, a team, a club, anywhere two people need someone to be fair.

how: Umar's letter to Abu Musa is taught in Islamic law and judging as a guide to a judge's conduct; its line on the claimant's proof echoes a principle Muslim jurists apply in courts.

games.q: what does “umar's letter on judging” mean?
o: a law code that fixed penalties for crimes
Umar's instructions to a judge on fairness and proof
a letter naming who would rule after Umar

s: Umar tells a judge to stand by his first ruling no matter what
returning to the truth after thinking again is better than staying in a wrong.
the letter says the one who makes a claim must bring the proof
and the one who denies takes an oath.
equal treatment, in the letter, includes where people sit and how you look at them
so the strong don't hope for favor and the weak don't despair.

games.q: your two kids each say the other broke the lamp. one is crying loudly; the other is quiet. what would Umar's letter have you do first?
o: give both the same calm face, and ask what each can show.
comfort the loud one first; the tears show who's hurt.
punish both the same so nobody feels singled out.
games.why: equal in how you look at them, and proof from the one who claims. the loudest side doesn't win, and the same punishment isn't the same as a fair hearing.

practice: Listen for two sounds, one on your left and one on your right. Give each the same attention and the same patience, turn by turn. When one pulls at you more, come back to the other.

wordCard.voice: Umar's letter on judging: to Abu Musa, a judge, on treating both sides as equals and letting proof, not volume, decide.

orig.note: Arabic: al-fahm al-fahm, understanding, understanding: Umar's repeated word to his judge.

carryVoice: The line to keep: equal before you, in your face and in your fairness. Day 1643, heard out.
